title: Workflow trust: Verification remains costly and contested
desc: Builds trust through authoritative sources, transparent signals, security and organizational change rather than demanding error-free AI.

kps.k: The cluster treats trust as a workflow property rather than a demand for error-free AI.
kps.d: The central proposition is that legal AI becomes usable when organisations place probabilistic output inside processes that prevent mistakes from reaching clients, courts or counterparties. Proponents compare supervised AI with associate work: lawyers delegate, inspect and remain accountable. They argue that acceptable performance relative to existing methods—not perfect reliability—can justify use, particularly where manual review is otherwise impracticable. This supports a copilot model; it does not establish that direct reliance on autonomous legal output is safe.

qs.q: One—which is kind of how Harvey is used—is human-in-the-loop, the same way that a partner would work with a team of associates.

kps.k: The principal disagreement concerns whether verification has resolved the adoption problem or remains a costly constraint.
kps.d: Some speakers say human review has made hallucinations manageable and shifted debate from whether to adopt AI to how to integrate it. Others call hallucinations a continuing trust gap, stress that fabricated cases or quotations differ from ordinary interpretive mistakes, and warn that checking legal reasoning may consume the anticipated productivity gain. Several sources also distinguish improving citation accuracy from new or unfamiliar reasoning failures. The evidence consists mainly of practitioner experience, intercepted internal errors and vendor claims; it does not provide comparative error rates or a general measure of verification cost.

qs.q: And so I would say we’ve actually—not we as in Harvey, but we as an industry—largely solved that trust problem.

kps.k: Trust-building mechanisms combine authoritative sources, transparent verification signals and security governance.
kps.d: Proposed safeguards include linking citations to authoritative databases, displaying citator signals, exposing research steps, allowing users to redirect agents, constraining LLMs with deterministic systems and requiring approval before actions. Enterprise deployment adds separate requirements for confidentiality, privilege, ethical walls, client permissions, data location, training rights and cross-organisation access controls. These mechanisms aim to accelerate verification and make systems auditable; vendors generally present them as risk reduction rather than guarantees, and several integrations or permissioning systems remain unfinished.

qs.q: And then within the final report itself, to your point on hallucinations, we include really clear visual signals for users around what might be a hallucination or not.
qs.a: Pablo Arredondo and Joel Hron on Reasoning Models, Deep Research, and the Future of Legal AI · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

qs.q: Now, we’ve got lots of rules and a ton of stuff around to limit that, and we believe we’re best in breed, but you still need to finally be able to verify, to check.
qs.a: LexisNexis CTO Greg Dickason on Agentic Legal AI, Protégé, Shepard’s Verify, and the Future of Legal Work · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

kps.k: Meaningful adoption requires behavioural and organisational change beyond purchasing licences.
kps.d: Sources distinguish enterprise sales and pilots from sustained use. Reported barriers include unfamiliar interfaces, established habits, professional-identity threat and fear arising both from poor performance and from possible replacement. Proposed responses include personalised starting points, rapid time to value, peer-to-peer training on live work, transparent leadership, voluntary early adoption, social proof and legal engineers who combine subject expertise with system knowledge. Evidence remains mixed: commentators report low use across many licence holders, while Harvey reports high daily engagement within the narrower subgroup using four or more product lines.

qs.q: One word of caution: adoption in terms of licenses is reportedly high, but actual use apparently remains relatively low.
qs.a: Harvey's Strategic Evolution · Academia · 2026

qs.q: Um so on the product side,  I think that's the most important piece is just making it very personalized and making it so the time to value is really short, like as fast as possible and then they'll go out and explore.
qs.a: Winston Weinberg (Harvey) — Sequoia Training Data Ep.33 · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

kps.k: The boundary between copilot and autopilot is task-specific and contested.
kps.d: Speakers anticipate broader delegation where tasks are bounded, repetitive and supported by relevant data, citing eDiscovery, document extraction, NDAs and contained documents-only disputes. Some predict unchecked execution of routine agreements within a few years. Others maintain that ethical responsibility requires lawyers to review work submitted to clients or courts and doubt that complex litigation or acquisitions will support end-to-end autonomy even over a decade. Bounded arbitration and settlement experiments retain human involvement, party consent or narrow use cases, so they do not demonstrate autonomous adjudication.

qs.q: I think there'll be certain activities that, like eDiscovery, you decide to delegate to technology more holistically because it gets to a level of performing where everyone says that's good enough.
qs.a: Ep 297: CoCounsel's Next Generation: Emily Colbert and Rawia Ashraf on Agentic AI for Lawyers · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

qs.q: But I think there will be low-level work—like, for example, NDAs—where the systems in the next couple of years will get to the point where you’ll probably just be able to say, “I want to enter into an NDA with this company.”  It’ll take all your historical data and their historical data and years of precedent, and it’ll be like, “We’ve generated this.

kps.k: The strategic ambition extends from individual assistance to redesigning legal-service delivery and collaboration.
kps.d: Vendors and AI-native firms increasingly describe legal AI as infrastructure for matter management, firm–client collaboration, customised playbooks and multi-step workflows, rather than merely a drafting assistant. AI-native providers propose integrating lawyers and engineers and rebuilding operations around model capabilities; Harvey emphasises secure collaboration between law firms and in-house legal teams. Competing forecasts remain open: stronger foundation models might enable in-house departments to insource outside-counsel work, while collaboration platforms might reinforce law firms and permit them to implement AI for clients. These are strategic bets, not demonstrated market outcomes.

qs.q: “When we first built the product, it was a co-pilot for individual lawyers,” Pereyra explained.
qs.a: Lessons from Slush 2025: How Harvey Is Scaling Domain-Specific AI for Legal and Beyond · Market & press · 2025

qs.q: One is there's one world where the foundation models get so good that in-house teams just bring in all of the outside council work, right?
qs.a: Gabe Pereyra — Harvey: agents as 'newspapers on the internet', training associates, and the bet on specialised firm systems · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

kps.k: Economic incentives may determine where adoption takes hold before technical capability alone does.
kps.d: Sources identify contingency work and fixed-fee, high-volume workflows as favourable entry points because efficiency can benefit clients while preserving or increasing provider earnings. By contrast, hourly billing can penalise faster completion, and partnership governance can discourage long-term investment when senior partners bear current costs but may not capture future returns. Some predict AI will enlarge firms or unlock previously uneconomic legal demand rather than simply replace labour; others note that these effects remain forecasts and that the billable hour has survived earlier technological changes.

qs.q: The plaintiff-side contingency model is one such area: everyone – the lawyers and their clients – benefits from tools that increase the chances of success and streamline the work.
qs.a: Law & Order: GPU · Market & press · 2025

qs.q: If efficiency gains allow lawyers to draft a complex contract or review a file in a fraction of the time, how do firms need to restructure their incentives so they aren’t punishing efficiency under this traditional hourly model?
qs.a: Why AI Will Create More Legal Work, Not Less: Filevine's Rizner and Anderson on Research, Access, and Human Judgment · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

kps.k: Claims that AI will improve access to justice remain promising but largely prospective.
kps.d: Commentators expect lower delivery costs, wider availability to smaller firms, greater legal-aid capacity, faster dispute processes and technology-enabled community practice. Reported current activity includes Harvey-assisted small-claims filing in Singapore, but broader claims about settlement, expanded civil-justice capacity and service to unmet legal need remain exploratory or aspirational. Sources also distinguish access-to-justice benefits from ordinary firm profitability, even though both may arise from the same efficiency gains.

qs.q: Um and one of the things we do there is basically if you are a citizen there, you can file a small claims uh with Harvey, right?
qs.a: Winston Weinberg — Harvey (CEO) on Wrapper Defensibility, Hiring Freezes and Fixed-Fee Legal Work · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: I’m also excited about the ways that it might help legal aid organizations or community legal services organizations that have far more requests for help than they have time or hours or humans to provide that help.
qs.a: How Will AI Tools Like ChatGPT 4.0 and Notebook LM Shape the Future of Law? — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2024

vlens.an: These curated AI-native-provider sources accept the principal proposition that legal-AI trust must be engineered through workflows rather than premised on error-free models, and they materially extend it with concrete organisational and delivery designs. Their common emphasis is on embedding AI within redesigned operations: integrating lawyers with engineers, retaining lawyer or user direction, constraining probabilistic models through deterministic systems, and requiring approval before action. They also reinforce the synthesis’s claim that adoption depends on organisational and economic conditions, including partnership investment incentives and the ability to build operations around improving model capabilities. There is material internal variation. Garfield addresses trust safeguards most directly, presenting architectural constraints, transparency and user approval as risk mitigation rather than elimination; however, its review mechanism relies substantially on clients checking facts, not necessarily lawyer verification. Berrent frames trust through lawyer-directed AI and a software-first client experience, but her claimed transformation remains prospective. Daniels focuses primarily on partnership incentives, lawyer–engineer integration and ambitious workflow offloading, offering little direct evidence about verification costs or security governance. Across the sources, projected economic expansion, adoption and automation benefits are strategic expectations rather than demonstrated general outcomes.

qs.q: The reason why we incorporated our own law firm and have our lawyers who are using our product sitting next to our engineers is because we don't want AI to just be doing 10% of their workflow.
qs.a: Ryan Daniels — Crosby (AI-native law firm) · AI-native providers · 2025

qs.q: And it's not autonomous—the user has to approve each action before the system takes it.
qs.a: Garfield Law: Inside the World's First AI-Native Law Firm — full episode transcript · AI-native providers · 2025

vlens.an: The academia-and-research source accepts the proposition that trust and meaningful adoption are properties of workflow integration and organisational behaviour, rather than consequences of licence purchases or error-free performance alone. It materially extends the proposition by proposing professional-identity threat as a two-sided adoption barrier: unreliable AI prompts distrust, while highly reliable AI may provoke fear of replacement. It also characterises engagement as bimodal rather than uniformly weak—many lawyers reportedly make little use of Harvey, but users who cross a multi-product integration threshold become deeply engaged. Internal variation therefore lies between scepticism that Harvey has achieved workflow-transforming, use-level product–market fit and qualified evidence of intense use within a narrower, highly integrated subgroup. These claims do not establish the cost of verification or the effectiveness of particular safeguards, and the identity-threat mechanism is presented as a possible explanation rather than a demonstrated finding. This assessment concerns the supplied source, not academia and research generally.

qs.q: That creates a double bind with AI: if the tool isn't reliable enough, it makes mistakes, and lawyers don't trust it.
qs.a: Harvey's Strategic Evolution · Academia · 2026

qs.q: It's a sharp split: most lawyers barely touch the tool, but those who cross some threshold of integration become deeply embedded in it.
qs.a: Harvey's Strategic Evolution · Academia · 2026

vlens.an: This in-house counsel and legal-operations voice accepts the cluster’s principal proposition that trust should be built through governed workflows rather than by requiring error-free AI, and materially extends it to the relationship between corporate clients, law firms and other advisers. Niles adds concrete enterprise-governance requirements—visibility, observability, auditability and explainability—and argues that safeguards used for regulated workflows should govern cross-organisational legal work. He also reframes client AI prohibitions as potentially reflecting either innovation avoidance or justified uncertainty about how advisers will deploy AI, making trust dependent on accountable use as well as system performance. The position is nonetheless bounded: it is conceptual and based on reported practices, does not show that these mechanisms work in practice, and does not address the cluster’s central dispute over verification cost. Because the supplied evidence contains one curated source, it supports analysis of this perspective but not claims about the prevalence of this view among in-house counsel or legal-operations professionals.

qs.q: That’s also how you defend regulated workflows—and it should also apply to how law firms and clients work together.
qs.a: A Conversation with Sabastian Niles on the Legal Profession in the Agentic AI Era · In-house counsel · 2026

vlens.an: The curated legal-tech-vendor sources collectively accept the principal proposition that legal-AI trust is produced through governed workflows rather than by demanding error-free models. They materially develop it by specifying mechanisms across the deployment lifecycle: authoritative-source links and citator signals; visible research paths and human steering; specialist legal data and explicit uncertainty; security, privacy, privilege, ethical walls, selective permissions and client authorisation; and adoption measures such as personalised onboarding, peer-led learning, social proof and legal-engineering roles. The prevailing framing is copilot-oriented: lawyers remain accountable, while autonomy may expand only for bounded tasks with demonstrated performance. Material internal variation concerns verification. Some vendor speakers argue that human review has largely removed hallucinations as an adoption blocker and predict lighter review or unchecked execution for routine tasks; others stress that unfamiliar reasoning errors, fabricated quotations and inadequate drafts can make checking consume the expected productivity gain. Sources also differ in emphasis: some focus on accuracy and verification signals, others on upstream data governance, organisational behaviour or firm–client infrastructure, while one augmentation-focused source does not address workflow trust closely enough to establish a position. Much of the support remains based on product experience, vendor assertions, anecdotes and forecasts rather than comparative error rates or measured verification costs. Because these are curated sources, this synthesis describes the positions represented here and does not establish their prevalence among legal-tech vendors generally.

qs.q: And so I think these visual signals,  are intended to really drive the user towards understanding what can I trust, what can I not trust, what do I need to verify, what do I not.

vlens.an: Across this curated set, market analysts, consultancies and press sources generally accept the proposition that legal-AI trust depends on managed workflows rather than error-free models, and they materially develop it by identifying operational conditions for adoption. Their common reasoning is that probabilistic output can be useful when deployment is use-case-specific and supported by authoritative sourcing, human judgment, governance, security, permissions, approvals and accountability. Several also broaden the analysis beyond technical safeguards: experienced professionals may be needed for evaluation; personalised interfaces and hands-on use can reduce behavioural resistance; licence purchases do not prove daily workflow integration; and fee structures or reputational signals can shape adoption. Material variation remains. Some sources focus directly on evidence-linked RAG, data protection and risk avoidance, while others emphasise cross-organisational permissioning, ethical walls or decision authority. Others chiefly discuss adoption psychology, prestige-based trust or aligned economic incentives and therefore support only parts of the proposition. One source addressing wider access for smaller firms and prospective access-to-justice benefits leaves the workflow-trust question unresolved. Much of the evidence is strategic reasoning, reported experience or prediction rather than comparative measurement; in particular, these sources do not establish general verification costs, safeguard effectiveness or safe autonomous reliance.

vlens.an: This curated set of sources from regulators, courts and professional-body contexts accepts the cluster’s principal proposition that legal-AI trust is created through supervised workflows, governance and organisational change rather than by requiring error-free output. Collectively, the sources materially develop that proposition by identifying additional trust mechanisms: granular editing that preserves lawyer agency, transparent leadership, authoritative legal-content and document-management integrations, and role-specific limits on AI use in advocacy, judging and bounded dispute resolution. They also connect these controls prospectively to increased legal-aid capacity and judicial acceptance. Material internal variation concerns whether verification has already made hallucinations operationally manageable: Pereyra says supervised workflows have largely solved the adoption-related trust problem, whereas McCormack and Leonard describe fabricated authorities as a continuing and distinctive barrier, and the interview separately raises the possibility that checking legal reasoning can consume expected efficiency gains. Across the set, direct reliance remains more contested than copilot use, particularly for judging and complex legal work. Most claims about faster adoption, judicial acceptance and access-to-justice gains are expectations or anecdotes rather than measured outcomes; this curated evidence should not be treated as representative of all regulators, courts or professional bodies.

vlens.an: This access-to-justice and civil-society voice supports the proposition that legal AI should not be required to be error-free before it can be trusted. Its central reasoning is comparative and institutional: human lawyers and judges also make mistakes, and the legal system manages that fallibility through review rather than treating any error as disqualifying. It also connects trustworthy AI to a prospective public-interest benefit—freeing lawyers from routine work and enabling more community-facing practice. There is material variation within the source: McCormack directly advances the institutional-review argument, while the community-lawyering and jurisdiction-specific product claims are aspirational and do not establish performance, verification cost, or economic viability. The source therefore supports the cluster’s core workflow-trust proposition but does not materially develop its detailed safeguards, security governance, or evidence about whether verification remains too costly.

vlens.an: This traditional-law-firm source supports the proposition that legal-AI trust is created through workflow controls rather than by requiring error-free output. Kercher accepts hallucinations as a real professional risk, based partly on fabricated material he encountered in internal drafts, but treats that risk as manageable through substantive human verification, user training, hands-on oversight and improved awareness of system limitations. He also supports the proposition’s organisational-change element: adoption at Quinn Emanuel was encouraged through voluntary participation, one-to-one assistance and positive reinforcement rather than a firm-wide mandate. The main qualification is evidential rather than directional. His account relies on practitioner experience and a delivery anecdote, so it does not establish comparative error rates, the net cost of verification or general productivity gains. It also remains firmly within a copilot model in which lawyers check and remain accountable for outputs, rather than supporting autonomous reliance. Because the curated evidence contains one law-firm voice, it shows how this practitioner relates to the proposition and should not be treated as representative of traditional law firms generally.

elens.an: The 2023–2024 sources support the proposition that trust in legal AI depends on workflow controls rather than error-free models. Across this curated set, hallucinations are treated as a serious adoption barrier—especially because fabricated authorities differ from junior lawyers’ interpretive mistakes—but not necessarily as a reason to reject legal AI. The common response is supervised, professional-facing use supported by authoritative evidence, use-case selection, governance, data protections and interfaces that preserve lawyer control. Material variation concerns how far reliability had improved: McCormack and Leonard emphasise the continuing reputational and qualitative trust gap; Wakeling treats residual error as manageable when AI improves on otherwise impracticable manual review; and Harvey reports stronger citation grounding through a custom model while retaining a copilot framing. The evidence is uneven: the barriers and safeguards are principally practitioner judgments, Harvey’s reliability claims are vendor-reported, and predictions about accelerated adoption, productivity and legal-aid capacity are prospective rather than demonstrated. These qualifications reinforce the synthesis’s conclusion that verification remained contested rather than undermining its workflow-trust proposition.

elens.an: Within this curated 2025 evidence, the sources collectively accept the principal proposition that legal-AI trust must be engineered through workflows rather than based on error-free model output, and materially develop it with concrete adoption-at-scale mechanisms. These include authoritative-source links and citators, visible citation and research signals, human steering and approval, deterministic constraints, input governance, client authorisation, confidentiality and privilege controls, ethical walls, cross-organisational permissioning, structured matter data, and lawyer-led training and implementation. Common reasoning is that probabilistic systems can support bounded delegation if mistakes are intercepted and lawyers retain responsibility, while adoption also requires rapid practical value, credible leadership, suitable incentives and redesign of work rather than licence purchases alone. Material variation concerns how far these measures have solved adoption. Some practitioner and vendor accounts report growing confidence, wider delegation and successful bounded uses; others stress that verification may erase productivity gains, experienced lawyers are needed to evaluate complex work, hallucinations and changing failure modes persist, and key integrations or permissioning systems remain unfinished. The copilot–autopilot boundary is therefore task-specific: bounded document work may support broader delegation, but the sources generally preserve human judgment for complex work and client- or court-facing output. Strategic claims about AI-native delivery, firm–client infrastructure, profitability and access to justice are mostly forecasts, anecdotes or product ambitions rather than measured outcomes. The curated 2026 sources collectively accept the proposition that legal-AI trust is produced through supervised, governed workflows rather than error-free output, and materially develop it with concrete mechanisms. These include authoritative click-through verification and citator signals; security, privacy, ethical-wall and selective-data controls; approvals, accountability and auditability; personalised onboarding, peer-led learning and legal-engineering roles; and organisation-specific playbooks with escalation to lawyers. They also extend workflow trust beyond individual use to firm-wide deployment, firm–client collaboration and narrowly bounded dispute-resolution processes.

The principal internal variation concerns how far these arrangements have resolved the trust problem. Pereyra argues that human verification has largely removed hallucinations as a barrier to supervised adoption, while still acknowledging that checking legal reasoning may consume the productivity gain and that direct reliance remains unresolved. Dickason likewise treats residual probabilistic error and final verification as permanent, while Filevine’s speakers emphasise fabricated quotations and model-dependent judgment as reasons for persistent lawyer oversight. On autonomy, some predict unchecked handling of routine agreements once task-specific performance is demonstrated, but complex litigation and acquisitions remain firmly within a copilot model; settlement and arbitration examples retain party consent, narrow scope or human involvement. Adoption accounts also vary between low use among many licence holders and deep engagement among a narrower, highly integrated subgroup, with proposed explanations ranging from habits and interface friction to professional-identity threat. Claims about efficiency, firm growth, training acceleration and access to justice are mainly practitioner observations, vendor accounts or forecasts rather than quantified outcomes. This assessment characterises only the supplied curated sources and does not imply prevalence across legal professionals or vendors.
